bar: A brand-new candidate sees genuinely relevant jobs in their first session.

approach_decisions.content_vs_popularity_cold_start: content-based (skill overlap) primary, popularity blended in and used as the fallback when skills are missing - rejected pure popularity as the primary strategy since it doesn't differentiate candidates at all
approach_decisions.explicit_onboarding_vs_profile_inference: infer from signup skills - rejected a separate onboarding quiz as added friction directly opposed to this task's activation goal
approach_decisions.exploration: 2/10 slots reserved for weighted-random exploration beyond the top-ranked set, so the second session can already start personalising

never_empty_verification.scenario: no skills on file, full job data
FORCED FAILURE: job catalog completely empty/unavailable

true_floor_case: When the job catalog itself is completely empty, there is genuinely nothing to recommend - no ranking strategy can invent jobs that don't exist. This is NOT a bug in the recommender; it's the actual floor of what 'never empty' can mean. The correct mitigation lives one layer below this task's scope: the ONBOARDING UX should detect zero available postings and show a distinct 'we're launching in your area soon, here's how to get notified' state, rather than the recommender silently returning nothing. Flagged as a hand-off item to Frontend, not solved here, since it's a UX/product decision, not a ranking one.
known_limitations: Lift is measured via simulation (a modelled true-relevance function based on skill overlap with realistic self-report noise), not a real A/B test - the DIRECTION and mechanism (content-based beats popularity-only when skills are available) should transfer, but the exact lift percentage needs re-validation against a real online experiment before being used as a launch metric.
The 8% no-skills-on-file rate is an assumed onboarding drop-off rate, not measured from real signup funnel data in this environment.

Exploration slot selection here is a simple weighted-random sample, not a proper multi-armed-bandit policy (e.g. Thompson sampling) - sufficient to demonstrate the core concept, but a real implementation should use a policy that formally balances explore/exploit rather than a fixed slot count.
